pr_title: systemctl: warn if trying to disable a unit with no install info
pr_body:
Trying to disable a unit with no install info is mostly useless, so adding a warning like we do for enable instead of exiting silently. Notice that it currently still removes symlinks to the unit, and this behavior is preserved.

Closes #17695
Closes #17689
pr_comments: @keszybz Mind reviewing this when you have free time? 😉

uh, i am not convinced this is desirable. And I am prety sure this might trip up some people.

The thing is packaging scripts might automatically call "systemctl disable" on all unit files they remove. So far that was a NOP. Now this would become very noisy. I am not convinced it should be noisy.

hmm, and also, i am also not convinced it would ever be a good idea to warn about unit files that lack [Install] but that people manually linked into /etc. because frankly that's something I personally do all the time: write a quick unit file without [Install] and quickly symlink it in myself. I'd bet it's not just mean, but some orchestrator tools might do the same. When "systemctl disable" is called on such units this should not generate any warnings.
So I am not really convinced by this at all, this needs more consideration. i.e. some conditionalization or so.

> The thing is packaging scripts might automatically call "systemctl disable" on all unit files they remove. So far that was a NOP. Now this would become very noisy. I am not convinced it should be noisy.

Hmm, discussion on this was brought up in #17695, and I believe there is a actual need to tell people that this might not do what they are trying to. Also, I don't think that such packaging scripts should be the obstacle to this. (Plus, a workaround would be to disable all units altogether and the warning will be shadowed :)

> When "systemctl disable" is called on such units this should not generate any warnings.

Make sense.

Hmm, for some reason, the commit message only contains part of the interesting information, and the rest is in the pull request comments. Please put all the info in the commit message so that it ends up visible in git history.

Yeah, I think it's reasonable to do this. Based on the multiple bug reports over the years, it is a reliable source of user confusion.  We just need to figure out how to do this without causing undue breakage to existing workflows.

> i am also not convinced it would ever be a good idea to warn about unit files that lack [Install] but that people manually linked into /etc. because frankly that's something I personally do all the time: write a quick unit file without [Install] and quickly symlink it in myself.

That case is actually handled nicely with this patch: if there *is* an existing symlink, `systemctl disable` just prints a line about the symlink being removed. The warning would be emitted only if you call `systemctl disable` and it's a noop.

> The thing is packaging scripts might automatically call "systemctl disable" on all unit files they remove. So far that was a NOP. Now this would become very noisy. I am not convinced it should be noisy.

Yep, people would kill us if we started printing a 10 line error message for each `systemctl disable` in packaging scriplets for such units. If we do this change, we would need to adjust packaging scriptlets to not print an error. This would need to be controlled by a new option. (I don't have a good idea for the name. We already have a `--quiet` option, but it has a different meaning in this context: it suppresses the printing of the lines about which symlinks were created. Maybe `--relaxed` or `--noop-ok` or `--no-warn`.)

`src/rpm/systemd-update-helper.in` would need to be adjusted to use this option in appropriate places.

And we would need to tell people to use the option in other tooling if appropriate. This is something of a compat breakage, but we can't avoid it, if we want to do this change. The whole point is to start showing the warning *by default*, so erroneous causal use from the commandline gets the warning. If we print the warning, we still return 0, which means that tooling will still work despite the warning.

> Hmm, for some reason, the commit message only contains part of the interesting information, and the rest is in the pull request comments. Please put all the info in the commit message so that it ends up visible in git history.

Reworded to include what I considered necessary. Feel free to ask for more :p

> Yep, people would kill us if we started printing a 10 line error message for each systemctl disable in packaging scriplets for such units. If we do this change, we would need to adjust packaging scriptlets to not print an error. This would need to be controlled by a new option. (I don't have a good idea for the name. We already have a --quiet option, but it has a different meaning in this context: it suppresses the printing of the lines about which symlinks were created. Maybe --relaxed or --noop-ok or --no-warn.)

I personally prefer `--no-warn`.
@keszybz I've added option `--no-warn` for suppressing the warning.

Please add the information about the bug numbers to the commit messages:
`Fixes #1. Fixes #2.` or so.

issue_context.title: Unable to disable `systemd-modules-load.service`
issue_context.body:
With Debian Bullseye/testing and systemd 246.6-2, I am unable to disable the service unit *systemd-modules-load*, not required on my system.

    $ sudo systemctl disable systemd-modules-load.service
    $ echo $?
    0

It’s still hooked up, though.

    $ ls -l /lib/systemd/system/sysinit.target.wants/systemd-modules-load.service
    lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root 31 19. Nov 22:35 /lib/systemd/system/sysinit.target.wants/systemd-modules-load.service -> ../systemd-modules-load.service
comments:
This service isn't supposed to be disabled by the user. It doesn't do anything unless configured via modules-load.d.

If you really don't want it to run, mask it instead.
```
systemctl mask systemd-modules-load.service
```

> This service isn't supposed to be disabled by the user.

How should the user now that? It’d be great, if `systemctl` would gave corresponding feedback, and not return with success.

> It doesn't do anything unless configured via modules-load.d.

It clutters the logs, and despite not much, it still consumes tiny resources, which is bad if `/etc/modules-load.d` is not used on quite a few systems. So it should be possible to easily disable that service unit.

> If you really don't want it to run, mask it instead.
> 
> ```
> systemctl mask systemd-modules-load.service
> ```

Yeah, that is one way. I removed the symbolic link `/lib/systemd/system/sysinit.target.wants/systemd-modules-load.service` instead.

> I removed the symbolic link /lib/systemd/system/sysinit.target.wants/systemd-modules-load.service instead.

That symlink will be restored whenever you upgrade/reinstall systemd.
Yes, please use `systemctl mask` if you really want to disable the service.
It is a bug, when `systemctl` returns success, but did not do anything.. Please re-open.
OK. Let's document the behavior explicitly. #17695.
